excerpt: Hospitals, health insurers, Medicare and attorneys can all claim part of your settlement. Which liens apply, and how they are negotiated.
keyTakeaways: Liens from hospitals, health insurers, Medicare, Medicaid, workers' compensation carriers, and attorneys can significantly reduce your personal injury settlement. Georgia's provider lien statute (O.C.G.A. § 44-14-470) lets hospitals and medical practices place a lien on your claim; South Carolina has no hospital-lien statute, so providers there rely on contract. Federal liens from Medicare (42 U.S.C. § 1395y) take priority over state law. Workers' comp liens are governed by O.C.G.A. § 34-9-11.1 in Georgia and S.C. Code § 42-1-560 in South Carolina. An experienced attorney audits every lien, challenges invalid or unrelated charges, and applies every statutory reduction the lien holder must accept.

faqs.question: What is a lien on a personal injury settlement?
faqs.answer: A lien is a legal claim against your settlement or judgment by a third party who paid for expenses related to your injury. Common lien holders include hospitals, health insurers, Medicare, Medicaid, workers' compensation carriers, and attorneys. Valid liens must be satisfied before you receive your share of the settlement proceeds.

faqs.question: Can hospital liens reduce my personal injury settlement in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes. Georgia's hospital lien statute (O.C.G.A. § 44-14-470) allows hospitals to place liens on personal injury settlements for the reasonable cost of treatment. The lien attaches to any recovery from a third-party claim. However, these liens are often negotiable, and your attorney can work to reduce the amount owed.

faqs.question: How do medical liens work in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina has no hospital-lien statute, so a hospital or doctor cannot file a lien against your claim. A provider's right to be paid rests on your contract with it — including any assignment of benefits or letter of protection you signed — and it is negotiated like any other bill. The claims that do reach a South Carolina settlement are health-insurer subrogation (allowed only if your policy contains a subrogation clause, S.C. Code § 38-71-190), Medicaid (§§ 43-7-430, 43-7-440), Medicare, and workers' compensation (§ 42-1-560).

faqs.question: Does Medicare have a lien on my personal injury settlement?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under the Medicare Secondary Payer Act (42 U.S.C. § 1395y(b)), Medicare must be repaid the conditional payments it made out of any liability settlement, judgment or award, and its right overrides state law. Repayment is due within 60 days of Medicare's demand, with interest after that, and Medicare can collect from you or your attorney if the money is paid out first — so the Medicare claim must be resolved before funds are distributed.

faqs.question: Can my attorney negotiate liens to increase my take-home amount?
faqs.answer: Yes. Experienced personal injury attorneys routinely reduce liens by challenging invalid or unrelated charges, invoking Georgia's complete-compensation rule or South Carolina's statutory limits on health-insurer subrogation, applying the federal rule that limits Medicaid to the medical-expense share of a recovery, and using Medicare's fee-reduction, waiver and compromise procedures.

faqs.question: What happens if I ignore a lien on my settlement?
faqs.answer: Ignoring a valid lien has serious consequences. Insurers, workers' compensation carriers and Medicaid can sue to recover what they are owed (in Georgia, a hospital enforces its lien against the at-fault party or its insurer), and your attorney must hold disputed funds in trust until the claims are resolved. Medicare charges interest on unpaid demands, refers unpaid debts to the U.S. Treasury for offset, and can collect from your attorney; in South Carolina, continued Medicaid eligibility depends on cooperating with the agency's reimbursement claim.
